Complaint: Periumbilical discomfort progressing to right lower quadrant pain over 3 days, decreased appetite, mild nausea, one loose stool  

Analysis: The CT scan demonstrates a dilated appendix (14 mm) with peri‑appendiceal fat stranding and a small contained fluid collection, establishing the diagnosis of acute appendicitis with early (contained) perforation. All three experts agreed on this diagnosis, the need for emergent care, and that management falls under General Surgery. Consensus also identified the patient’s age, diabetes, coronary artery disease, and early perforation as major risk factors for peri‑operative complications. Divergence arose regarding the breadth of pre‑operative testing: Expert A advocated for a full cardiac work‑up including ECG and cardiac enzymes, whereas Expert B considered basic labs sufficient and viewed additional cardiac testing as optional. Expert A also suggested prophylactic antibiotics aimed at protecting the knee prosthesis, a recommendation not supported by Experts B or C. All experts concurred on the core immediate management—IV fluids, broad‑spectrum antibiotics, NPO status, and urgent surgical consultation—but differed on the extent of ancillary measures such as DVT prophylaxis and cardiac optimization.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT (already obtained), complete blood count, basic metabolic panel, serum lactate, coagulation profile, electrocardiogram, cardiac enzymes (troponin), renal function assessment for contrast clearance and antibiotic dosing, pre‑operative chest radiograph if indicated, assessment of beta‑blocker therapy, allergy history for antibiotics and contrast, and functional status evaluation.  

Conclusion: Acute appendicitis with early contained perforation in an elderly patient with significant comorbidities constitutes a surgical emergency that requires prompt operative intervention.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery  

Recommendations: Initiate immediate resuscitation with isotonic crystalloid fluids and keep the patient NPO. Begin broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobic organisms (e.g., piperacillin‑tazobactam or ceftriaxone plus metronidazole), adjusting for local resistance patterns and renal function. Obtain the full set of pre‑operative labs listed above, including ECG and cardiac enzymes, to stratify cardiac risk given known coronary artery disease; continue beta‑blockers peri‑operatively unless contraindicated. Review medication list for antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents and manage accordingly. Provide pharmacologic deep‑vein thrombosis prophylaxis (e.g., low‑molecular‑weight heparin) because of recent total knee arthroplasty and heightened thrombotic risk. Ensure tight glycaemic control throughout the peri‑operative period. Verify allergy status for both antibiotics and iodinated contrast; select alternative agents if needed. Consider intra‑operative assessment for cecal pathology that could suggest underlying malignancy; obtain postoperative pathology of the appendix and, if indicated, follow‑up colonoscopy. Plan postoperative monitoring for signs of peritonitis, intra‑abdominal abscess, sepsis, wound infection, and cardiac events. Arrange early mobilization and coordinate with physical therapy to address functional status and facilitate rehabilitation after both abdominal surgery and recent knee replacement.  

Notes: The contained fluid collection indicates a localized perforation that may evolve; close postoperative surveillance with repeat imaging is advisable if clinical status worsens.

Complaint: Eye fatigue, dryness, and mild headache that worsen with prolonged computer use; symptoms improve on weekends.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on a diagnosis of computer vision syndrome (digital eye strain) based on the temporal relationship to screen time, normal visual acuity, intact extraocular movements, and lack of red‑flag findings. The consensus is that the condition is benign, self‑limited, and does not require emergent intervention, and that ophthalmology is the appropriate specialty for further evaluation if symptoms persist. Points of divergence include: Expert B emphasized scheduling a routine ophthalmology follow‑up within 2–4 weeks, whereas Experts A and C considered follow‑up only if self‑care measures fail. Expert C highlighted the possibility of subtle refractive or binocular vision abnormalities despite 20/20 acuity, while Experts A and B regarded additional testing as unnecessary unless symptoms persist. Expert A mentioned blue‑light filtering glasses, an outlier suggestion not strongly supported by evidence. Expert B listed early glaucoma in the differential to ensure thoroughness despite a normal exam.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No immediate diagnostic tests are required. If symptoms do not improve with self‑care, consider: basic subjective refraction, tear break‑up time or Schirmer test for dry‑eye assessment, near‑point of convergence testing for accommodative or convergence insufficiency, and a comprehensive ophthalmic examination to detect subtle refractive or binocular vision issues. An ergonomic workstation assessment may be performed by occupational health personnel.  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with computer vision syndrome (digital eye strain). The condition is self‑care appropriate and can be managed initially with non‑pharmacologic measures, with ophthalmology referral reserved for persistent or atypical cases.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology  

Recommendations: Implement the 20‑20‑20 rule (every 20 minutes, look at an object 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and take a brief 5‑minute break each hour. Optimize workstation ergonomics: screen at eye level, appropriate viewing distance (about 20‑30 inches), adequate ambient lighting, and reduced glare. Use preservative‑free artificial tears as needed for ocular surface comfort. Encourage adequate hydration, regular physical activity, and proper posture to lessen musculoskeletal strain. Review systemic medications and medical history for anticholinergic drugs or autoimmune conditions (e.g., Sjögren syndrome) that may exacerbate dry eye. If symptoms persist after 2–4 weeks of diligent self‑care, obtain a comprehensive eye exam including refraction and dry‑eye testing; consider near‑point convergence testing for accommodative or convergence insufficiency. Counsel the patient on red‑flag symptoms (sudden vision loss, flashes, floaters, eye pain, diplopia, photophobia, or neurological deficits) and advise prompt evaluation should they arise. Blue‑light filtering glasses may be tried, but their benefit is not well‑established; prioritize ergonomic adjustments over optical filters. If tension‑type headache does not improve with ocular measures, address it separately with appropriate headache management strategies.  

Notes: Monitor for any evolution of symptoms; schedule a follow‑up ophthalmology appointment within 2–4 weeks if there is no improvement or if new ocular signs develop.

Analysis: The patient’s 40‑year smoking history, chronic productive cough, and acute worsening of symptoms after an upper‑respiratory infection are classic for an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, a component of COPD. No red‑flag features (hemoptysis, fever, chills, weight loss, severe dyspnea at rest) are reported, supporting a non‑emergent outpatient approach. Experts converged on the need for pulmonology involvement and outpatient evaluation. Divergence arose regarding antimicrobial therapy and inhaled corticosteroids: one expert advised reserving antibiotics for purulent sputum and deferring steroids until COPD is confirmed, while another suggested they could be considered if sputum becomes purulent or COPD severity warrants. Both agree on bronchodilator use, smoking‑cessation counseling, and the importance of imaging and spirometry. Additional considerations highlighted include high pack‑year risk for COPD and lung cancer, unknown vaccination status, possible occupational exposures, need for baseline vitals and oxygen saturation, COVID‑19 testing, prior exacerbation history, family history, eligibility for low‑dose CT lung‑cancer screening, and the role of smoking‑cessation pharmacotherapy.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Chest radiograph; baseline spirometry with post‑bronchodilator testing; pulse oximetry; measurement of vital signs including respiratory rate and oxygen saturation; COVID‑19 rapid antigen or PCR test if indicated; consider complete blood count and sputum culture only if sputum becomes purulent or patient fails to improve; low‑dose CT chest for lung‑cancer screening if COPD is confirmed and patient meets USPSTF criteria.  

Conclusion: The presentation is most consistent with an acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis within COPD, without emergent red flags. Outpatient evaluation by pulmonology is appropriate, with targeted diagnostics to confirm COPD, exclude pneumonia or malignancy, and guide further therapy.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology  

Recommendations: Arrange outpatient pulmonology appointment within the next few days. Obtain chest X‑ray and perform spirometry to confirm airflow limitation. Measure vital signs and pulse oximetry at the visit; if oxygen saturation is < 92 % on room air, consider supplemental oxygen and earlier follow‑up. Initiate a short‑acting bronchodilator trial (e.g., albuterol inhaler) for symptom relief. Provide intensive smoking‑cessation counseling and offer pharmacotherapy such as varenicline or nicotine‑replacement therapy. Review and update influenza and pneumococcal vaccinations; administer if indicated. Counsel the patient on avoidance of occupational and indoor pollutants. If COVID‑19 exposure or symptoms are present, test accordingly. Reserve antibiotics for cases where sputum becomes purulent, fever develops, or a bacterial infection is otherwise suspected. Defer inhaled corticosteroids until spirometry confirms COPD and the patient meets criteria for their use based on severity and exacerbation frequency. Schedule follow‑up in 1–2 weeks to reassess symptoms; if no improvement, obtain sputum culture, consider CBC, and evaluate need for CT chest if the chest X‑ray is abnormal or if lung‑cancer risk remains high. If COPD is confirmed, assess eligibility for low‑dose CT lung‑cancer screening per USPSTF guidelines.  

Notes: Document vaccination history, occupational exposures, prior exacerbations, and family history of lung disease for future risk stratification.

Analysis: All three experts agree that the presentation is most consistent with an acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) manifesting as viral rhinitis. The patient is afebrile, well‑appearing, and lacks red‑flag findings such as fever, purulent nasal discharge, facial pain/pressure, ear pain, dyspnea, or cervical lymphadenopathy, supporting a self‑limited viral process. Consensus exists that no immediate diagnostic testing or specialist referral is required. Minor areas of divergence include the breadth of the differential: Expert B added COVID‑19 infection, non‑allergic irritant rhinitis, and emphasized pandemic‑related considerations; Expert A and C listed allergic rhinitis, early bacterial sinusitis, and influenza as alternative possibilities. Expert B also noted that ENT referral may be considered only for persistent or complicated rhinitis, whereas Experts A and C did not mention referral criteria. All agree on supportive care and the need for patient education on red‑flag symptoms.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None at this visit; clinical diagnosis is sufficient. Consider rapid COVID‑19 antigen testing only if recent exposure, high community prevalence, or patient concerns arise.  

Conclusion: Acute viral upper respiratory infection (common cold) – self‑limited, no urgent intervention required.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: General Medicine  

Recommendations: Advise the patient to increase fluid intake, obtain adequate rest, and use saline nasal irrigation for symptomatic relief. Over‑the‑counter oral antihistamines or topical decongestants may be used short‑term if nasal congestion is bothersome, avoiding use beyond three days to prevent rebound congestion. No antibiotics are indicated. Emphasize strict hand hygiene, routine mask use while symptomatic, and avoidance of close contact with vulnerable individuals, especially given her role as a daycare teacher. Inquire about seasonal allergy history and known triggers; if allergic rhinitis is suspected, consider a trial of intranasal corticosteroid or antihistamine spray for recurrent symptoms. Review pregnancy status before selecting any medication; avoid decongestants in early pregnancy if possible. Ask about smoking or second‑hand smoke exposure and counsel on avoidance. Screen for immunocompromising conditions (e.g., HIV, chronic steroid use) that would alter management. Verify recent travel, known COVID‑19 exposure, and current influenza activity; ensure COVID‑19 vaccination is up to date and discuss the potential need for testing or isolation if exposure is identified. Provide clear return precautions: seek care if fever >38 °C develops, nasal discharge becomes purulent, facial pain or pressure arises, ear pain occurs, sore throat worsens with exudates, or any difficulty breathing or new lymphadenopathy appears. If symptoms persist beyond ten days without improvement, arrange follow‑up for possible secondary bacterial infection.  

Notes: The patient’s occupational exposure increases the likelihood of viral transmission; reinforce infection‑control measures in the daycare setting.

Age: 5 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Pruritic erythematous papules with central puncta on forearms and lower legs, onset over 24 hours after outdoor play  

Analysis: All three pediatric experts converged on papular urticaria (insect‑bite hypersensitivity) as the most likely diagnosis. The key clinical features supporting this are the acute appearance of multiple small papules with central puncta on exposed skin after outdoor exposure, the absence of systemic symptoms, and lack of signs of infection or severe allergy. Consensus was uniform regarding the non‑urgent nature of the condition, the appropriateness of primary‑care management, the limited differential list (including scabies, contact dermatitis, acute urticaria, viral exanthem, early bacterial infection, early Lyme disease, folliculitis, and papular eczema), and the red‑flag features that would mandate escalation. No expert recommended routine laboratory testing; all agreed testing is reserved for atypical presentations or emergence of red‑flag signs. The only minor variation was the reported confidence level (Experts B and C expressed high confidence, Expert A reported neutral confidence), but this did not affect the clinical conclusions. Additional considerations raised during the rounds—such as possible atopic predisposition, pet exposure, recent lawn mowing or standing water, tick exposure, and tetanus vaccination status—were not points of disagreement but are incorporated into the management plan.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: No routine tests are indicated. Consider skin scraping, complete blood count, or Lyme serology only if lesions become atypical, if red‑flag signs develop, or if there is a history suggestive of tick exposure.  

Conclusion: Papular urticaria (insect‑bite reaction) – a benign, self‑limited dermatologic condition that can be managed in the outpatient pediatric setting.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics  

Recommendations: Provide symptomatic relief with a low‑potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., hydrocortisone 1 %) or calamine lotion applied twice daily, and an oral second‑generation antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine) as needed for pruritus. Use cool compresses and keep the child’s nails trimmed to minimize excoriation. Advise the caregiver to monitor for red‑flag signs (fever, rapidly spreading erythema, purulent drainage, lymphangitis, airway compromise, generalized angioedema, systemic malaise, arthralgia, or neurologic changes) and to seek prompt medical attention if any develop. Return for follow‑up in 3–5 days if lesions have not improved, or sooner if worsening occurs. Educate the family on preventive measures: apply EPA‑registered insect repellent (e.g., DEET or picaridin) before outdoor activities, dress the child in long sleeves and pants, avoid peak biting times (dawn and dusk), eliminate standing water, maintain yard hygiene, and regularly inspect pets for fleas and ticks. Inquire about a personal or family history of atopy, prior similar episodes, and recent pest infestations in the home. Verify tetanus immunization status in case secondary bacterial infection (impetiginization) develops; initiate appropriate antibiotics only if clinical evidence of infection appears. If lesions are atypical, recurrent, refractory to therapy, or if diagnostic uncertainty persists, arrange referral to dermatology.  

Notes: Emphasize that secondary bacterial infection is the most common complication; early signs include increased warmth, pain, or purulent discharge. Rarely, early herpes simplex or molluscum contagiosum may mimic central puncta but are unlikely given the history.

Age: 24
Sex: Female
Complaint: Dysuria, urinary frequency, right flank pain, fever, rigors, nausea, vomiting
Analysis: The presenting features of fever >102 °F, rigors, tachycardia, borderline hypotension, vomiting, marked costovertebral‑angle tenderness and a urinalysis showing leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria and bacteriuria are classic for acute pyelonephritis. All three experts agree that the infection meets criteria for emergent care and that systemic signs constitute red‑flag features indicating possible early sepsis. Experts A and C classify the illness as a complicated urinary tract infection because of prior recurrent UTIs, systemic involvement and hemodynamic changes; Expert B describes it as acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis, noting the absence of known obstruction. The consensus therefore is acute pyelonephritis with features of a complicated infection due to systemic response and prior history. All agree that initial management should occur in the Emergency Department, that blood and urine cultures must be obtained before antibiotics, that empiric broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation are required, and that inpatient admission is indicated because of vomiting and the need for IV therapy and monitoring. Imaging is not required emergently in a classic presentation but should be obtained if the patient fails to improve within 48‑72 hours or if an obstructive process is suspected. The experts concur on the likely pathogen (Escherichia coli) and on a 10‑14‑day antibiotic course with post‑treatment follow‑up and evaluation for anatomic abnormalities.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: CBC with differential, serum electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, serum lactate, blood cultures, urine culture, urinalysis, pregnancy test (already negative), bedside vital‑sign monitoring, intravenous access, and, if clinical response is inadequate after 48‑72 hours, renal ultrasound or contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
Conclusion: Acute pyelonephritis, most likely complicated by systemic inflammation and prior recurrent infections, requiring emergent evaluation and inpatient management.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease
Recommendations: Obtain a focused allergy history before selecting empiric antibiotics; initiate early goal‑directed sepsis therapy with 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus, repeat assessment of hemodynamics, and serum lactate measurement; draw blood and urine cultures prior to antibiotic administration; start empiric IV broad‑spectrum coverage (e.g., ceftriaxone 1 g q24 h or cefepime 2 g q8 h) with adjustment for allergy or local resistance patterns; provide antipyretics, analgesics and anti‑emetics; admit for continuous vital‑sign monitoring, IV fluid replacement, and IV antibiotics; reassess clinical response at 48‑72 hours and obtain renal imaging if fever persists, pain worsens, or renal function declines; after culture results, de‑escalate to the narrowest effective agent and complete a total of 10‑14 days of therapy; arrange outpatient follow‑up with primary care or urology within 1‑2 weeks; obtain a post‑recovery renal ultrasound to evaluate for obstruction, stones, reflux or other anatomic abnormalities; consider urologic referral and prophylactic strategies if recurrent UTIs continue; educate the patient on hydration, prompt reporting of worsening symptoms, and safe sexual practices while on oral contraceptives.
Notes: Ensure adequate hydration given recent vomiting; monitor for progression to septic shock with serial blood pressures, heart rate, mental status and lactate trends; although pregnancy test is negative, remain vigilant for gynecologic emergencies that can mimic flank pain; absence of hematuria does not exclude nephrolithiasis, especially radiolucent stones; assume immunocompetence unless further history suggests otherwise.

Complaint: Burning and aching pain on the right side of the chest for 5 days, followed by erythema, a maculopapular rash that progressed to clear vesicles, then pustulation, ulceration, and crusting; associated headache and malaise.  

Analysis: All three experts converged on a diagnosis of herpes zoster involving a right thoracic dermatome, agreeing that the condition is non‑emergent but requires timely antiviral therapy within 72 hours to reduce the risk of post‑herpetic neuralgia and other complications. Dermatology was unanimously identified as the primary managing specialty, with primary‑care coordination and infectious‑disease consultation reserved for systemic or disseminated disease. The differential diagnosis list (herpes simplex virus infection, contact dermatitis, impetigo, allergic drug eruption, bullous pemphigoid, cellulitis, cutaneous T‑cell lymphoma, disseminated zoster) was consistent across experts. Red‑flag features (ocular involvement, disseminated rash, severe immunosuppression, neurologic deficits, secondary bacterial infection, and in elderly patients headache/malaise suggesting possible CNS involvement) were also uniformly recognized. Consensus held that clinical diagnosis is sufficient; laboratory confirmation (PCR, DFA, or Tzanck smear) is reserved for atypical or immunocompromised cases. Treatment recommendations (oral antivirals, multimodal analgesia, gentle wound care) and follow‑up timing (1–2 weeks) were identical. Points of divergence included Expert C’s identification of missing assessment elements (standardized pain‑severity scale, consideration of corticosteroids, documentation of exact dermatomal level, evaluation for zoster sine herpete, and monitoring for mental‑health impact) and a stronger emphasis on infectious‑disease involvement for antiviral guidance. Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Age: 28  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Continuous generalized tonic‑clonic seizure lasting >12 minutes despite two benzodiazepine doses (IM midazolam 10 mg, IV lorazepam 4 mg)  

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified the presentation as refractory convulsive status epilepticus, a life‑threatening emergency that demands immediate airway protection, rapid second‑line antiseizure therapy, and intensive supportive care. Consensus was reached on the need for Emergency Medicine to lead the initial resuscitation with early Neurology consultation, continuous EEG monitoring, and ICU admission. A point of divergence emerged regarding the subclinical specialization: Expert A favored Neurology as the primary specialty, whereas Experts B and C designated Emergency Medicine. This difference reflects the dual nature of the condition—neurological in pathology but requiring emergent emergency‑department interventions. The panel agreed on the red‑flag features (prolonged seizure, benzodiazepine failure, hyperthermia, hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, possible infection, medication non‑adherence) and on a comprehensive differential diagnosis that includes psychogenic non‑epileptic seizures, metabolic disturbances, CNS infection, structural lesions, toxin exposure, and autoimmune encephalitis. All experts endorsed the same diagnostic work‑up and therapeutic steps; the outlier suggestions (routine serum pregnancy testing and inclusion of autoimmune encephalitis) were already incorporated in the consensus recommendations.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Point‑of‑care glucose meter, arterial blood gas analyzer, bedside pulse‑oximeter, cardiac telemetry monitor, rapid‑sequence intubation kit, mechanical ventilator, active cooling devices, intravenous infusion pumps, laboratory panel (CBC, basic metabolic panel, renal and liver function tests, serum lactate, creatine kinase, toxicology screen, levetiracetam level, blood cultures, serum β‑hCG), non‑contrast head CT scanner, emergent EEG equipment, lumbar puncture set (if infection suspected).  

Conclusion: Refractory convulsive status epilepticus in a 28‑year‑old woman with known epilepsy, precipitated by missed levetiracetam doses and possible infection, requiring emergent airway protection, second‑line antiseizure medication, and ICU admission with continuous EEG monitoring.  

Emergency type: Requires emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Emergency  

Recommendations: 1. Perform immediate rapid‑sequence intubation with mechanical ventilation, 100 % oxygen, and continuous cardiac and pulse‑ox monitoring. 2. Initiate active cooling to reduce core temperature below 38 °C. 3. Administer a rapid IV loading dose of a second‑line antiseizure drug (e.g., fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg, valproate 30 mg/kg, or phenobarbital 15–20 mg/kg) while preparing for continuous anesthetic infusion (midazolam or propofol) if seizures persist. 4. Transfer the patient to the ICU for continuous EEG, cardiac telemetry, frequent neurologic and respiratory assessments, and serial metabolic labs. 5. Obtain the following investigations emergently: point‑of‑care glucose, CBC, BMP, renal and hepatic panels, serum lactate, CK, toxicology screen, levetiracetam level, arterial blood gas, blood cultures, serum β‑hCG, non‑contrast head CT, emergent EEG, and lumbar puncture if infection is not contraindicated. 6. Monitor renal function to adjust levetiracetam dosing and avoid accumulation. 7. Serially measure CK and electrolytes to detect rhabdomyolysis and metabolic acidosis. 8. Provide aggressive hydration and consider bicarbonate therapy if severe acidosis develops. 9. Implement aspiration pneumonia surveillance; start empiric antibiotics if clinical or radiographic evidence of pneumonia appears. 10. Address social determinants of health: arrange social work consultation to resolve medication access and insurance barriers before discharge. 11. Maintain continuous cardiac telemetry to detect arrhythmias secondary to hypoxia and autonomic instability. 12. Keep autoimmune encephalitis on the differential; if seizures remain refractory despite standard therapy, consider autoimmune work‑up (e.g., serum/CSF antibody panels). 13. Ensure serum pregnancy testing is performed promptly to guide the choice of antiseizure medications and potential teratogenic considerations.  

Notes: Early collaboration between Emergency Medicine and Neurology is essential; EM manages airway, breathing, circulation, and initial drug administration, while Neurology directs second‑line and refractory seizure management, EEG interpretation, and long‑term epilepsy care.

Age: 31 years  
Sex: Female  
Complaint: Six‑month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge, breast tenderness, secondary amenorrhea (6 months), progressive headaches, infertility, decreased libido, and vaginal dryness.  

Analysis: All three experts concur that the clinical picture—marked hyperprolactinemia (500 µg/L), galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, and a sellar mass measuring approximately 1.1 × 1.6 × 2.1 cm on contrast‑enhanced MRI—most strongly indicates a prolactin‑secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma), specifically a macroadenoma given its size (>1 cm). The normal visual fields, absence of optic chiasm compression, and lack of acute neurologic deficits support a non‑emergent status. Consensus also places primary management under Endocrinology.  

Points of minor divergence:  
- Expert A emphasized a broader differential (non‑functioning adenoma, hypothalamic lesions, drug‑induced hyperprolactinemia, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure, chest wall lesions) while noting prolactinoma as the leading diagnosis.  
- Expert B highlighted specific red‑flag findings that would convert care to emergent (sudden visual loss, optic chiasm compression, pituitary apoplexy, adrenal insufficiency) and recommended routine assessment for these.  
- Expert C stressed the need to exclude assay interference by macroprolactin and suggested repeat prolactin measurement with a macroprolactin assay.  

Overall, the converged reasoning affirms a macroprolactinoma requiring prompt but non‑emergent endocrine therapy, with vigilant monitoring for the outlined red‑flag signs.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the brain with contrast (already performed), formal automated visual field testing (perimetry), comprehensive pituitary hormone panel (prolactin repeat with macroprolactin assay, ACTH, cortisol, GH, IGF‑1, LH, FSH, estradiol, TSH, free T4), baseline renal and hepatic function tests, and routine pregnancy testing before initiating therapy.  

Conclusion: The patient has a prolactin‑secreting macroadenoma (prolactinoma) presenting with hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, infertility, and progressive headaches, without current optic chiasm compression or acute neurologic compromise.  

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care  
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology  

Recommendations: Initiate dopamine‑agonist therapy, preferably cabergoline (starting dose 0.5 mg weekly, titrated to prolactin normalization), with bromocriptine as an alternative if cabergoline is contraindicated. Counsel the patient on expected side‑effects (nausea, orthostatic hypotension, rare valvulopathy) and the importance of adherence. Schedule follow‑up prolactin measurement at 4‑6 weeks, repeat MRI at 6‑12 months, and repeat visual field testing at baseline and sooner if visual symptoms develop. Perform the full pituitary hormone panel now to identify any co‑existing deficiencies; replace deficient hormones (e.g., glucocorticoids) before or during dopamine‑agonist initiation if indicated. Order a macroprolactin assay to rule out assay interference, especially if prolactin levels do not correlate with clinical response. Analysis: The panel unanimously identified an acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by inability to absorb oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone during viral gastroenteritis. All experts agreed that the refractory hypotension, severe hyponatremia (118 mEq/L), hyperkalemia (6.4 mmol/L) with ECG changes, hypoglycemia (52 mg/dL), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.1 mg/dL), and altered mental status constitute life‑threatening complications that mandate emergent, ICU‑level care. Consensus was reached that Emergency Medicine should lead the initial resuscitation while Endocrinology provides co‑management of hormonal replacement and chronic planning. A minority view favored Endocrinology as primary lead; the final decision reflects the majority opinion favoring Emergency Medicine leadership. Additional considerations raised during the rounds—risk of adrenal hemorrhage, need for bedside adrenal ultrasound, assessment for other autoimmune polyglandular disorders, potential pregnancy, CYP3A4‑inducing drug interactions, and the importance of anti‑emetic therapy—were incorporated into the recommendations.
Required diagnostic equipment/tests: continuous cardiac telemetry, arterial line if needed for blood pressure monitoring, 12‑lead ECG, bedside ultrasound of the adrenal glands, point‑of‑care glucose, arterial blood gas, serum electrolytes, BUN/creatinine, serum cortisol, ACTH, lactate, blood cultures, urine cultures, stool studies for infectious gastroenteritis, chest X‑ray as clinically indicated.
Conclusion: Acute adrenal crisis secondary to missed glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement in the setting of viral gastroenteritis, with secondary hypovolemic/ septic‑like shock and metabolic derangements.
Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology
Recommendations: Immediate 1 L isotonic saline bolus followed by rapid infusion (250–500 mL/h) while monitoring urine output; administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV now then 100 mg every 8 hours (or continuous infusion 200 mg/24 h) to provide glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity; treat hyperkalemia with calcium gluconate, insulin‑glucose, and nebulized β‑agonist; give 50 % dextrose IV for hypoglycemia; initiate norepinephrine if MAP remains <65 mmHg after fluids and steroids; add fludrocortisone orally once the patient can tolerate intake; obtain repeat electrolytes, glucose, BUN/creatinine, cortisol, ACTH, ABG, lactate, and cultures every 2–4 hours initially; perform bedside adrenal ultrasound to evaluate for hemorrhage; consider empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics if clinical signs of bacterial sepsis develop; provide anti‑emetic medication to facilitate oral medication absorption; assess pregnancy status and adjust steroid dosing if pregnant; review current medications for CYP3A4 inducers and hold or adjust as needed; screen for autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (thyroid antibodies, fasting glucose, HbA1c); admit to ICU for continuous cardiac telemetry, invasive blood pressure monitoring, frequent laboratory reassessment, and titration of vasopressors; upon stabilization, educate the patient on sick‑day rules, prescribe an emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kit, recommend a medical alert bracelet, and arrange prompt endocrinology follow‑up for maintenance dose optimization and further autoimmune work‑up.

Analysis: All three experts unanimously identified necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg as the diagnosis, emphasizing the classic triad of severe pain out of proportion, rapid progression, and systemic signs of sepsis, supported by crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, gas on CT, and a LRINEC score of 10. Consensus was reached that the condition is a surgical emergency requiring operative debridement within hours and that General Surgery must lead definitive management after initial stabilization by Emergency Medicine. The experts agreed on the need for aggressive fluid resuscitation, vasopressor support, tight glycemic control, ICU admission, tetanus prophylaxis, and a broad‑spectrum antibiotic regimen (vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, clindamycin) with renal dose adjustments. Points of divergence arose from Expert C, who changed the service activation order to emphasize Emergency Medicine’s role in activation and highlighted several missing considerations: assessment for peripheral arterial disease, early Infectious Disease involvement, potential use of hyperbaric oxygen, evaluation for compartment syndrome and need for fasciotomy, planning for repeat debridements and multidisciplinary wound care, verification of tetanus immunization status, and serial monitoring of inflammatory markers such as CRP and procalcitonin. Expert C also noted that the questionnaire was insufficient because these aspects were not addressed.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Computed tomography of the affected leg (already performed) to delineate gas and fascial involvement; bedside high‑frequency ultrasound to assess fluid collections; repeat complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel for trend monitoring; serial lactate measurements; blood cultures (two sets) before antibiotics; wound or intra‑operative tissue cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) and histopathologic biopsy; coagulation profile; arterial Doppler studies or ankle‑brachial index to evaluate peripheral arterial disease if time permits; assessment of tetanus immunization status; consider magnetic resonance imaging only if it will not delay surgery; serial C‑reactive protein and procalcitonin levels to gauge response.

Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg requiring emergent surgical debridement.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care
Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Initiate immediate sepsis bundle in the emergency department with 30 mL/kg isotonic crystalloid bolus, obtain blood cultures, and administer empiric vancomycin, piperacillin‑tazobactam, and clindamycin with dosing adjusted for the patient’s creatinine of 2.4 mg/dL. Begin insulin infusion for tight glycemic control and monitor glucose hourly. After fluid resuscitation, start norepinephrine infusion for persistent hypotension, aiming for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg. Provide tetanus prophylaxis with tetanus toxoid and, if immunization status is unknown or incomplete, consider tetanus immune globulin. Transfer the patient to the intensive care unit for continuous hemodynamic, renal, and electrolyte monitoring; correct hyponatremia cautiously, evaluating for SIADH versus volume depletion. Evaluate the limb for compartment syndrome; if clinical signs persist despite resuscitation, perform emergent fasciotomy in addition to debridement. Arrange urgent operative exploration by General Surgery within 1–2 hours of diagnosis; intra‑operative tissue biopsy and cultures should be obtained. Plan for repeat debridements every 24–48 hours until all necrotic tissue is removed, and involve plastic surgery early for potential reconstructive needs. Consult Infectious Disease promptly for antimicrobial stewardship and potential de‑escalation based on culture results. Assess peripheral arterial disease with bedside Doppler or ABI to inform surgical planning and postoperative perfusion. If hyperbaric oxygen therapy is available and the patient is hemodynamically stable, consider it as an adjunct after the initial debridement. Monitor lactate every 2 hours until it trends down, and follow serial CRP and procalcitonin to assess inflammatory response. Maintain vigilance for deep‑vein thrombosis; if suspected, obtain duplex ultrasonography and weigh anticoagulation against postoperative bleeding risk. Continue goal‑directed sepsis care, including repeat lactate measurement, source control verification, and organ‑support optimization.

Notes: The prior oral cephalexin regimen is insufficient for the polymicrobial and anaerobic spectrum typical of necrotizing fasciitis and should be discontinued. All interventions must be coordinated to avoid delays in definitive surgical source control. Documentation of time points for antibiotics, fluids, vasopressors, and operative start is essential for quality metrics.

Vignette:
A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.

winner_protocol:
Age: 20 years  
Sex: Male  
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the third and fourth toes on both feet for 2 weeks, associated with maceration and mild erythema; no pain, swelling, or systemic symptoms.  

Analysis: All three experts agreed that the presentation is classic for interdigital tinea pedis (athlete’s foot) in a young athlete who uses communal showers. The clinical picture is mild, localized, and lacks red‑flag features such as severe pain, extensive erythema, vesicles, bullae, fever, or underlying immunosuppression, supporting a non‑urgent management pathway. Consensus was reached that self‑care is appropriate, although Expert B initially favored a non‑emergent outpatient visit; the panel ultimately aligned on self‑care given the typical appearance and availability of effective over‑the‑counter therapy. Regarding specialty involvement, all experts identified Dermatology as the preferred subclinical specialty for definitive diagnosis, while acknowledging that primary‑care clinicians can manage straightforward cases; Expert C’s emphasis on primary‑care alone was noted but did not alter the consensus. The differential diagnosis list converged on several conditions (interdigital candidiasis, contact dermatitis, psoriasis/eczema, erythrasma, bacterial intertrigo, dyshidrotic eczema) with scabies retained only as a remote possibility by Experts A and B; Expert C later removed it as clinically irrelevant for this case.  

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for typical presentation; clinical diagnosis is sufficient. If uncertainty arises or treatment fails, perform a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings, consider fungal culture, and optionally a Wood’s lamp examination to evaluate for erythrasma.  

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis (dermatophyte infection) affecting the third and fourth web spaces bilaterally.  

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate  
Subclinical specialization: Dermatology  

Recommendations: Initiate an over‑the‑counter topical antifungal (e.g., terbinafine 1% cream, clotrimazole 1% lotion, or miconazole) applied twice daily for 2–4 weeks, ensuring the full course is completed even if symptoms improve earlier. Keep the interdigital areas dry; thoroughly dry feet after washing and consider using an absorbent powder. In communal shower settings, wear flip‑flops and change socks daily; use breathable footwear and treat shoes and socks with antifungal spray or powder to reduce environmental reservoirs. Advise the patient to avoid topical corticosteroids, which can mask the infection and lead to tinea incognito. Monitor for signs of secondary bacterial infection (new pain, swelling, warmth, purulent discharge) and seek medical evaluation if these develop. If no improvement after 2 weeks of appropriate topical therapy, or if red‑flag features appear, obtain a KOH preparation and consider referral to Dermatology for confirmation and possible oral antifungal therapy. Counsel the patient on the risk of recurrence due to perspiration and shared facilities; encourage teammates to practice similar hygiene measures and consider screening close contacts if an outbreak is suspected.  

Notes: The panel’s aggregate ratings indicate high efficiency (mean 9), strong resource adequacy (mean 9), and perfect alignment with the original problem (mean 10). Confidence in the classification and management plan is high (9/10).
